Mr. AR Yusuf with Mr. Manzur-Ur-Rahim, Advocates  ------- For the Plaintiff.

full_judgment:
3. In the instant case the defendant No. 1 MY Birba through its local agent filed an application for return of the plaint on the grounds that the plaintiff in this suit has challenged the validity of the declaration of General Average in question and has sought declaration to the effect that declaration of general average is illegal and not binding upon the plaintiff. But this Court in its Admiralty Jurisdiction is not competent to adjudicate the validity of the general average declaration and has no jurisdiction to make the declaration sought by the plaintiff herein. The authority of this Court in its Admiralty Jurisdiction is conferred and limited by the provisions of Admiralty Court Act, 1861. But the said Act does not confer any jurisdiction to this Court to decide any dispute arising out of the General Average Act and as such this Court has no jurisdiction to entertain and try the present suit in its Admiralty Jurisdiction. In a word, the prayer of defendant No. 1 is that there is no cause of action for institution of such a suit and a suit for such a declaration does not come within the purview of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861. I have heard the arguments of both sides on this preliminary point of maintainability of the present suit instituted in its present form. 

 4. At the very outset, Mr. Aminur Rahman Yusuf (AR Yusuf) has read out before me section 135A of the Transfer of Property Act and with it he has referred to a decision reported in 16 DLR (SC) 61 (East and West Steamship Co. Vs. Queensland Insurance Co.) showing the locus standi of the present plaintiff to institute the present suit. In that decision their Lordships of the Supreme Court of Pakistan held that in a case of Marine Insurance the Insurer having paid up loss sustained by the assured and being subrogated to the position of the assured is entitled to sue tortfeaser ie the person who has caused the loss, in his own name. Mr. Yusuf has cited another decision of this Court reported in 43 DLR 548, Sadharan Bima Corporation Vs. Bangladesh Shipping Corporation, wherein this Court held that the insurer being not the owner or assignee or consignee of the goods is not entitled to file a suit under section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861. It appears that at the time of hearing of that case this provision of section 135A of the Transfer of Property Act and the decision reported in 16 DLR (SC) were not placed before this Court. However, on some other grounds that suit was found not maintainable. So, in the present case the plaintiff insurance corporation being subrogee is entitled to file the suit under the Admiralty Court Act, 1861, as the right as well as remedy gets transferred to the subrogee by operation of law. 

 5. The plaintiff being subrogee has invoked the jurisdiction of this Court under Admiralty Court Act. Mr. Rafiq-Ul-Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for defendant No. 1 M. V. Birba, submits that the present suit in its present form having no cause of action cannot be entertained either under section 6 or any other sections of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861. Mr. Yusuf, on the other hand, has referred to different sections, namely, sections 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12, particularly; he has referred to section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act. Section 6 of the said Act runs as follows: 

 7. Mr. Yusuf has referred to the case of Albert David (Bangladesh) Limited Vs. M/s NedIloyd Lijnen BV, Rotterdam, 34 DLR 356. He placed reliance upon the observation of his Lordship that the Admiralty Jurisdiction of High Court Division can be traced back to clause 26 of the Charter of 1774 by which power was given to the Supreme Court of Bengal to hear, examine, try and determine all causes, civil and maritime and "all pleas of contracts" and ''all matters and contracts" which in any manner whatsoever relates to freight or money due for ships hired and let out, transport-money, maritime usury, trespass, injuries, complaints, damages and matters, civil and maritime, whatsoever, between merchants, owners and proprietors of ships and vessels, employed or used within jurisdiction or between others contracted 'done, had or commenced contracted, in, upon or by the sea, or public rivers, or ports. He further submits that jurisdiction of High Court Division is derived from the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act of 1891 and the Court of Admiralty Act of 1861 of England. But in the same decision it is held by his Lordship that under the Act of 1891 the High Court Division of this Court was declared as Court of Admiralty.This Court exercised the same jurisdiction as the High Court of England exercised in 1890 under the Admiralty Court Act of 186l. In order to understand the matter more clearly let me quote his Lordship's observation which runs as follows: 

 "So far as the present action for non- delivery of the plaintiffs cargo is concerned the jurisdiction of this Court is not derived from the Letters Patent of 1862 or that of 1865, but from the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act (India) of 1891 and the Court of Admiralty Act, 1861 of England. The latter Act is not on our statute book but it is administered in view of the combined operation of sub-section (2) of section 2 of the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act 1890 of the British Parliament and the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act (India) 1891, the latter Act being revised by the Bangladesh Laws (Revision and Declaration) Act, 1973 (Act VIII of 1973) is now on our statute book. It is true that if the revised Court of Admiralty Act of 1891 is read in isolation then it would not give any idea as to the nature and extent of the Admiralty jurisdiction of this Court, but it is to be read in its historical perspective. Under the Act of 1891 the High Court Division of this Court was declared as the Court of Admiralty. This Court exercises the same jurisdiction as the High Court of England exercised in 1890 under the Admiralty Court Act of 186l." 

 9. Mr. Yusuf has further referred to the case of At-Sayer Navigation Co. Vs. Delta International Traders Ltd., 34 DLR (AD) 110. In that case the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court held that for loss of market due to longer voyage through breach of contract, the owner of the goods is entitled to sue for damages. It has further been held that for damages on account of late delivery of goods carried by the ship, the principle of calculating loss for late delivery as in the case of transit by land will be applicable. Relying upon this decision Mr. Yusuf has referred to paragraphs 7 and 8 of the plaint, Mr. Yusuf stated that in bill of lading No. 2, out of 132 drums of palm oil the importer got only 15 drums; in bill of lading No. 1, out of 527 drums the importer got delivery of 48 drums; in bill of lading No. 5, out of 57 cartons of Polyester Yarn the importer got 52 cartons and in bill of lading No. 23, the importer got 19 cartons out of 25 cartons. In these two paragraphs Mr. Yusuf has tried to show the short delivery of the cargoes, but nowhere the value of these alleged short-delivered goods was assessed and nowhere any assessment was made as regards the quantum of damage for long delay in discharging the goods. No prayer was made for a decree for any compensation for any alleged damage. 

 10. Mr. Yusuf submits that the claim of the plaintiff as well as short delivery of the imported goods are very much there in the plaint and as such the claim of the plaintiff comes under section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act. This contention of Mr. Yusuf has no basis inasmuch as no claim for damage and compensation with regard to damage or short-delivered imported goods is made in the plaint itself, which is the main ingredient of section 6 of the above Act for invoking jurisdiction of this Admiralty Court. So, the decision reported in 34 DLR is not in any way helpful to Mr. Yusuf. 

 11. Mr. Rafiq-Ul-Huq has referred to section 1(q) of the Administration of Justice Act, 1956. In that section the provision of general average was specifically inserted. Though that Act is not applicable in our country, yet Mr. Rafiq-Ul-Huq submits that since Admiralty Court Act of 1861 docs not contemplate and include the provision of general average, the Administration of Justice Act, 1956 inserted specifically that declaration of general average in section 1 (g). So, by reference, he wanted to submit that general average is not contemplated under the Admiralty Court Act, 1861. 

 12. In this case I do not like to mention anything on merit although Mr. Yusuf argued it at length. In two other Admiralty suits, namely, Admiralty Suit No. 4 of 1982 and Admiralty Suit No. 6 of 1982 this Court recently delivered judgments decreeing the suits. In those two suits the plaintiffs prayed for decree for damages and compensation against the self-same defendant No.1 the vessel which loaded the goods of the plaintiffs from Singapore and, violating the terms of the contracts, the vessel went to Madras and thereafter the defendant No. 1 vessel reached Chittagong after about 8 months and few days and those two cases were decided on their own merits. Fundamental difference in between the instant suit and other two suits decreed is that damage and compensation were assessed and the specific prayer were made for a decree for damage done to the goods by the carrier. But in the present case there is no assessment of any damage or compensation and there is no prayer for decree for any amount as regards damage and compensation of goods damaged. In view of the above, I am of opinion that the suit as framed in the plaint of the present case and the prayer made in the plaint are quite distinguishable from the above two admiralty suits, and as such I find that the present suit is not maintainable either under section 6 or any other sections of the Admiralty Court Act of 1861. There is no cause of action shown as regards any damage done to the goods and there was no prayer for decree for compensation for the damaged goods. Decree claiming for damage and compensation must be prayed for in an admiralty suit, and a prayer for declaration that the declaration of general average is illegal and void may be made as additional, supplementary or ancillary or consequential prayer along with the main prayer for decree for compensation for the damage done to goods by the carrier during the voyage. But such a declaration as made in the present case does not independently come within the purview of any of the provisions of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861. So, I find no substance in the contention of Mr. Yusuf. 

 13. Mr. Yusuf further submits that if the present suit is not directly maintainable under section 6 or any other sections of the Admiralty Court Act, the plaintiff is entitled to institute such a suit under clause 26 of the Charter establishing the Supreme Court at Fort William in Bengal dated 6th March, 1774. Clause 26 of the said Charter of 1774 has given wide jurisdiction to this Court 10 entertain any suit regarding any maritime claim and crime. In reply, Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq submits that the contention of Mr. Yusuf is absolutely erroneous. He has referred to section 9 of the Act establishing High Court of Judicature at India dated 6th August. 1861. By section 9 of the above Act the jurisdiction given to the Supreme Court by the Charter of 1774 was abolished. In 1861 the Admiralty Court Act came into force. On 14th May 1962 the Letters Patent for the High Court of Judicature at Fort William in Bengal came into force. Here, by section 31 the Admiralty Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court as Admiralty Court was taken away. On 28th December, 1865, the Letters Patent for the High Court of Judicature at Fort William in Bengal came into being and in this Letters Patent, 1865 the High Court of Judicature was given all powers civil, criminal and admiralty. Section 32 of the Letters Patent of the year 1865 has given to the High Court of Judicature at Fort William the jurisdiction to exercise all civil and maritime powers as may be exercised by the High Court of Admiralty or Vice-Admiralty and also such jurisdiction for other maritime cases arisen in India as may be exercised by the said Court, Mr. Huq has then referred to section 3 of Law Reforms Ordinance of the year 1978. Under section 3 of the Law Reforms Ordinance, 1978, the Letters Patent of 1865 was totally repealed. Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq submits that under these circumstances, even if, before 1978, that is before promulgation of Law Reforms Ordinance, Mr. Yusuf could have faintly argued that such a matter regarding declaration of maritime claim is maintainable before this Admiralty Court but after the repeal of Letters Patent vide Law Reforms Ordinance of 1978, Mr. Yusuf has no scope to argue that under clause 26 of the Charter of 1774 this Court has jurisdiction to entertain such a suit. 

 "There was no further extension of Admiralty jurisdiction of the High Court in England by statute or otherwise over cargo claims or over contract of carriage of goods till 1920, so that at the time when the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act, 1890 was enacted, the High Court in England in its Admiralty jurisdiction could exercise jurisdiction in those matters only under the Admiralty Court Act, 1861. Therefore, it transpires, that this Court can have jurisdiction to entertain the present action, if at all, only under the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 and under no other statute or principle." 

 15. The upshot of the aforesaid decision is this that if damage done to the goods and if compensation for that damage is prayed for and if the cause of action and the claim arise for such compensation for damage then such a suit under the Admiralty Court Act is maintainable, and all maritime claims and disputes can be raised before this Admiralty Court only under the provisions of the Admiralty Court Act of 1861, and in no other law. I respectfully agree with his Lordship's view to the fact that the only law under which the admiralty suit is to be entertained by this Court is the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 and under no other law. So, the second submission of Mr. Yusuf fails. 

 16. Defendant No.1 has filed this application for return of the plaint. In the Code of Civil Procedure, Order VII. rule 10 contains the provision of return of plaint. He has not prayed for rejection of the plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. But under Order XLIX, rule 3(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure the return of the plaint in Admiralty Suit under Order VII, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not permissible. In the case of M/s. Saleh Steel Industries Ltd. and another Vs. TSS Pacific Abeto and others, 1983, BLD (HC) 104, the Admiralty Court (MH Rahman, J.) allowed rejection of plaint on the ground that no cause of action had arisen under the provisions of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 for institution of that suit. In this connection regarding return or rejection of plaint in an Admiralty Suit under Order VII, rules 10 and 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq has referred to the case of M/s Saleh Steel Industries Limited Vs. TSS Pacific Abeto and others, 35 DLR (AD) 188. In that case their Lordships, after considering the provisions of Order VII, rules 10 and 11 read with Order XLIX, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, held that this Admiralty Court has no jurisdiction to reject a plaint in an Admiralty Suit under Order VII, rule 11(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure. But their Lordships further held that the Admiralty Court is conferred with power to return a plaint under section 151 read with sections 117 &141 of the Code of Civil Procedure, although Order XLIX, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure puts restriction upon High Court Division for returning the plaint to the plaintiff in the exercise of its ordinary or extraordinary original civil jurisdiction. In that decision their Lordships also held that the rejection of the plaint under Order VII, rule 11 (a) by the Admiralty Court is not permissible. Since rejection of plaint is not permissible as held by their Lordships. Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq submits that for abundant caution he has prayed for return of the plaint relying upon the decision of their Lordships in that case. In this connection I may quote Order VII, rules 10 &11 and Order XLIX, rule 3(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 22. However, Mr. Huq submits that in the aforesaid judgment of 35 DLR (AD) case, this rule II, clause (a) of Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure was taken and considered. But clause (a) is no where in Order XLIX, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure which puts embargo in rejecting or returning plaint in Admiralty suit. Mr. Huq asserts that it must be clause (b) or at best, in a wrong way, it should be clause (d), but in no way it can be clause (a) of rule 11 of Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure. Since Order XLIX, rule 3(1) does not contain any barring clause upon clause (a) of rule 11 of Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure, Mr. Huq, submits, he could have prayed for rejection of the plaint under Order VII, rule 11(a) of the Code as the present case does not disclose any cause of action for instituting a suit under section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act But taking abundant caution in view of the above decision of the Appellate Division he has filed this application for return of the plaint, which the Appellate Division allowed in the aforesaid reported case under section 151 read with sections 117 and 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
